checks.claim: Key: moss is a producer (a small green plant that photosynthesizes)
checks.note: Grokipedia: mosses are 'small, non-vascular land plants'; the green leafy gametophyte 'is photosynthetic and independent'.

checks.claim: Moss grows in damp shady places, on forest floors and rocks (stem scene)
checks.note: 'moist, shaded environments like forests'; 'forest floors, rock surfaces'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: mushrooms are not producers; a mushroom is a fungus, not a plant, cannot make its own food
checks.note: 'Unlike plants, fungi lack chlorophyll and cannot perform photosynthesis'; distinct from plants and animals; mushrooms are fungal fruiting bodies.

checks.claim: Context: a mushroom (here on a fallen log) is a decomposer
checks.note: Fungi are 'indispensable as decomposers (saprotrophs)'. Some fungi are mycorrhizal partners or parasites instead, but a mushroom fruiting from a fallen log is a wood-decay saprotroph, so the scene makes the label true.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: snails and beetles are consumers, not producers
checks.note: Animals are heterotrophs/consumers. Some forest-floor snails and beetles eat dead leaves or wood (detritivores), but none is a producer, so both stay wrong. 'Eat other living things' is a fair 5th-grade gloss.

checks.claim: Context: 'like other plants it makes its own food from sunlight'
checks.note: True of plants generally at this level (a handful of parasitic plants such as dodder do not photosynthesize; not worth a change at grade 5).

checks.claim: Key: an animal that eats only plants is a herbivore
checks.note: Grokipedia: a herbivore 'primarily consumes plant material'; a strict (obligate) herbivore eats only plants. Key holds.

checks.claim: Stem: a wild rabbit eats grass, leaves and twigs, and only plants
checks.note: 'Rabbits are strict herbivores'; diet 'grasses, forbs, bark, and twigs'. The rabbit is a clean example.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: carnivore, omnivore, decomposer
checks.note: Carnivores eat animals; omnivores eat both; decomposers are fungi and bacteria. All wrong.

checks.claim: Context: 'A herbivore eats only plants, and rabbits, deer and caterpillars are herbivores'
checks.note: Deer and caterpillars are the standard textbook herbivores (Grokipedia Herbivore lists 'elephants, deer, rabbits, and caterpillars'; NatGeo: 'Deer... are herbivores'), but the sentence ties them to 'eats ONLY plants', and neither group strictly does: white-tailed deer were videotaped deliberately eating songbird nestlings in North Dakota (Pietz and Granfors 2000, American Midland Naturalist, USGS), and a small number of caterpillars are predators (Hawaiian Eupithecia; the harvester butterfly's aphid-eating larva). Rabbits are true strict herbivores. Minor, but these are animals that break the simple label. Suggested fix: 'A herbivore eats plants, and a rabbit eats nothing else. Deer and most caterpillars are herbivores too.' (or list 'rabbits, elephants and most caterpillars').

checks.claim: Context: decomposers are mostly fungi and bacteria
checks.note: NGSS LS2.A: 'Some organisms, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead organisms'.

checks.claim: Key: in grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake, the frog and the snake are carnivores
checks.note: 'Adult frogs are predominantly carnivorous' (insects); Grokipedia Snake: 'Snakes are obligate carnivores, relying exclusively on animal prey'. Tadpoles graze plants, but the chain's frog eats a grasshopper, so it is an adult.

checks.claim: Grasshopper eats plants (herbivore), so choices naming it are wrong
checks.note: 'primarily herbivorous insects'; 'some species exhibit limited omnivory, such as scavenging dead insects' only under plant scarcity. In this chain it eats grass, so herbivore is right.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Only the snake' (top-predator misconception)
checks.note: The frog eats an animal, so it is a carnivore too; 'only the snake' is wrong.

checks.claim: Feeding links are real: grasshoppers eat grass, frogs eat grasshoppers/insects, snakes eat frogs
checks.note: Snake page: 'many colubrid snakes consume small rodents, frogs, and birds'; the Grasshopper page names frogs among its predators.

checks.claim: Key: the mice (seeds and caterpillars) are the omnivores
checks.note: 'Deer mice are omnivorous'; seeds are a major food; arthropods eaten 'include spiders, caterpillars'. The stem states both foods, so the answer follows from the stem as well as from real mice. (NatGeo's food-web page calls grassland mice herbivores, but the stem's mice eat caterpillars, so no conflict.)

checks.claim: Wrong choice: deer (leaves and acorns) are herbivores
checks.note: Deer browse leaves and twigs and eat mast such as acorns. Context scopes it: 'In this forest the deer... eat only plants', which matches the stem's stated diet.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: caterpillars (leaves) are herbivores
checks.note: 'Most caterpillars are herbivorous, voraciously consuming leaves'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: owls (mice and small birds) are carnivores
checks.note: Owls 'are predominantly carnivorous predators'; prey includes mice and birds; no plant food.

checks.claim: Feeding links real: owls eat deer mice
checks.note: 'Deer mice are important prey for snakes (Viperidae), owls (Strigidae)'.

checks.claim: Key: the arrow rabbit -> fox shows energy passing from the rabbit to the fox
checks.note: Trophic links are 'edges pointing from prey to predators'; Generation Genius: 'The arrows show the direction the energy is transferred'.

checks.claim: Stem example grass -> rabbit -> fox is a real chain
checks.note: 'grass consumed by rabbits, which are then eaten by foxes'; red foxes are named rabbit predators on Grokipedia Rabbit.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: energy fox -> rabbit; rabbit runs away; fox is bigger
checks.note: Arrows show energy direction from food to eater, not escape or size. All three wrong.

checks.claim: Context: students often draw the arrows backwards
checks.note: Teaching sources report students 'often reverse the direction of the arrow to show that an animal is eating' (Wisconsin DNR handout, as quoted in search results; NABT 2018 also reports students misidentify the direction of energy flow).

checks.claim: Key: all of a pond's food chains together are a food web
checks.note: 'A food web consists of all the food chains in a single ecosystem.'

checks.claim: Stem: most animals eat more than one kind of food
checks.note: 'Most animals eat more than one thing.'

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a food pyramid; context says 'A food pyramid is a guide to healthy eating'
checks.note: The choice is still wrong, but the context gives only the nutrition meaning. In ecology 'food pyramid' is also a name for the ecological (energy) pyramid: Wikipedia, 'also trophic pyramid, Eltonian pyramid, energy pyramid, or sometimes food pyramid'. That pyramid shows the amount of living things or energy at each feeding level, not all the chains joined, so it is not a food web either. A pupil who has met the ecology sense is told something incomplete. Fix: context 'A food pyramid is a guide to healthy eating (in science, a pyramid of feeding levels shows how much food or energy each level holds, not who eats whom)', or swap the distractor for one with a single meaning.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a life cycle is the stages a living thing grows through
checks.note: 'the complete sequence of developmental stages that an organism undergoes'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: a habitat is the place where a living thing lives
checks.note: 'the specific set of resources and environmental conditions in a given area'.

checks.claim: Key: frogs die -> more insects (prey released)
checks.note: The TEKS 5.12B frog-disease example: the insects the frogs ate 'exploded in numbers' and the frog-eaters went hungry. Textbook answer and ecologically sound; in Central America amphibian die-offs have been linked to unchecked mosquitoes.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: fewer insects
checks.note: Removing a predator raises its prey; 'fewer insects' is not defensible in this closed web.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: more herons
checks.note: Herons are named frog predators; losing their food lowers, not raises, their numbers. Context's 'their numbers fall' is the right prediction for this web (real herons also eat fish, which the context's 'much of their food' allows).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: more plants
checks.note: More insects eat more plants, so plants would fall, not rise. Wrong.

checks.claim: Context: a change to one member spreads through the whole web
checks.note: 'When one link in the food web is threatened, some or all of the links are weakened or stressed.'

checks.claim: Key: more rabbits -> less grass left, because it is eaten faster
checks.note: Overgrazing: grazing 'removes plant cover faster than it can recover'; Yellowstone elk example. Textbook and true.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: no change, because grass makes its own food
checks.note: Making its own food does not stop grass being eaten; plant-eater numbers and plants are linked.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: more grows, because hawks eat the rabbits
checks.note: The stem says far more rabbits are born; the hawks' eating does not make grass grow more. Wrong reason, wrong result.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: less is left, because hawks eat it too
checks.note: Hawks are carnivorous birds and eat no grass; right result, false reason, so wrong.

checks.claim: Feeding links real: rabbits eat grass, hawks eat rabbits
checks.note: Grasses in the diet; 'hawks (e.g., red-tailed hawk...)' among predators.

checks.claim: Key: most open-ocean producers are tiny floating algae (phytoplankton)
checks.note: NOAA: 'Phytoplankton are microscopic marine algae'; 'float in the upper part of the ocean, where sunlight penetrates'; 'the base of several aquatic food webs'. Grokipedia Phytoplankton: they do 'the majority of oceanic primary production'.

checks.claim: Is 'algae' fair when phytoplankton include cyanobacteria?
checks.note: Fair at grade 5. NOAA itself calls phytoplankton algae, and Grokipedia notes cyanobacteria are 'also termed blue-green algae'. By output, the cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus make about 25% of ocean net primary production (Flombaum et al. 2013, PNAS, via BioNumbers https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?id=112104), so true algae still do most of it; by number of cells Prochlorococcus dominates the nutrient-poor open gyres, but as 'blue-green algae' that still fits the key, and no choice names bacteria. Optional: the context could say 'tiny floating algae and their cousins, the blue-green bacteria' if the lead wants full precision.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: tiny floating animals (zooplankton) are consumers
checks.note: Zooplankton are mostly heterotrophic drifters that graze phytoplankton.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: schools of small fish are consumers
checks.note: Fish are consumers.

checks.claim: Wrong choice and context: no seaweed grows on a seabed miles down in the dark
checks.note: Seaweed needs light; grows on hard substrates in the photic zone; deepest records 'up to 268 meters'. Free-floating Sargassum does live in open-ocean patches, but the choice says 'on the seabed' and Sargassum is not most of the producers, so the choice stays wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: the open ocean is miles deep
checks.note: Average depth 3,682 m (12,080 ft), about 2.3 miles.

checks.claim: Context: each phytoplankter is too small to see on its own; they drift near the sunlit surface
checks.note: 'microscopic'; typical size 0.2 to 200 micrometres. (A few large diatoms and colonies are just visible, but 'each... on its own' is fair.)

unit_notes: 9 questions: 7 ok, 2 uncertain, 0 error. Both uncertain items are context wording, not keys: (1) 3fc69f2de6 ties deer and caterpillars to 'eats only plants' though deer have been filmed eating songbird nestlings and a few caterpillars are predators; (2) 7a1b94bfde explains 'food pyramid' only as the nutrition guide, though in ecology it is also a name for the energy pyramid. Every key and every 'what happens next' prediction (frogs die -> more insects; more rabbits -> less grass) is the textbook answer and also true; no other choice is defensible. Moss as producer and mushroom as decomposer check out. 'Tiny floating algae' for open-ocean phytoplankton is NOAA's own wording and fair at grade 5 (cyanobacteria are ~25% of ocean production and are traditionally 'blue-green algae').
